extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, aesthetics, and humor theory; anyone analyzing or classifying instances of comic effect
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Alexander Bain's account of the ludicrous to decide whether an instance is comic by testing (a) whether something dignified is degraded and (b) whether the circumstances excite no other strong emotion. Includes procedural steps and diagnostic questions for analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occasion of the ludicrous (defining formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The occasion of the ludicrous is the degradation of some person or interest possessing dignity, in circumstances that excite no other strong emotion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Bain's core definitional criterion: comic effect arises specifically when dignity or importance is lowered, and only when no stronger competing emotion is evoked. Use the formula as the primary test when classifying an instance as comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of dignity to degrade
rubrics_metrics.description: The target must possess (or claim to possess) some form of dignity, importance, or seriousness; the downfall of someone already low produces no laughter; only the fall of the high.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms of dignity that can be degraded include personal dignity (status, manner, self-presentation), institutional dignity (church, government, profession), subject-matter dignity (sacred topics, weighty themes), logical dignity (the form of correct argument), and aesthetic dignity (the elevated style). Examples: a bishop slips (comic) vs a child slips and is hurt (not comic); a pretentious speaker's mispronunciation (comic) vs a humble person's (less comic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety condition: absence of other strong emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: The degradation must occur "in circumstances that excite no other strong emotion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for pity, indignation, fear, disgust, or sorrow; if any of these emotions arise they swamp the comic effect. If degradation produces real suffering, perceived injustice, threat, repugnance, or genuine grief, classify the instance as non-comic regardless of the dignity-fall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast between heights and depths (magnitude criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic is essentially a contrast between heights and depths; the audience perceives the dignified frame then the lowered actuality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The greater the height fallen from, the greater the comic force, provided the safety condition holds. Bain phrases this as comic force being "in proportion to the height fallen from," suggesting a graded/scale-like assessment of comic intensity based on magnitude of the fall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded cases (what is not comic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Situations where degradation is not comic: degradation that wounds (excites pity), degradation that outrages justice (excites indignation), mere lowness without prior height (no contrast), mere height without fall (sublime, not comic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exclusions serve as anti-patterns. Even if dignity or solemnity is present, if the event evokes pity, anger, fear, disgust, or genuine sorrow, or if there is no perceptible prior height to contrast with, the instance should be ruled non-comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to superiority and relief theories
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic is both a kind of superiority feeling and a release of mobilized respect: it is superiority specifically over the dignified-fallen and relief when respect mobilized against something important is deflated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to situate Bain's criterion among broader theories: treat comic responses as feelings of superiority (Hobbes) constrained to dignified targets, and as relief (Spencer) in contexts where respect/seriousness has been mobilized and then released. This helps explain why some superiority/relief cases are not comic unless the dignity/fall pattern is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural test for diagnosing comic instances
rubrics_metrics.description: A four-step test Bain gives for any candidate humor instance: 1) Identify what dignity/importance is in play. 2) Identify the degrading event. 3) Check: do the circumstances excite pity, indignation, fear, disgust, or grief? 4) If yes → not comic; if no → comic in proportion to the height fallen from.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this checklist in order as an analytic procedure. The third step is decisive: presence of any listed strong emotion overrides the comic classification. If the test yields 'comic', quantify strength by assessing the height-from-which-one-falls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic questions for analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions to guide judgment: What dignity (personal, institutional, intellectual, aesthetic) is being degraded? How great is the height being fallen from? Do the circumstances admit any other strong emotion (pity, anger, fear, disgust)? Is the audience's relation to the dignity such that they can enjoy its degradation rather than mourn it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions as prompts when annotating or scoring instances of humor. The audience relation question is crucial: the same degradation may be comic for one audience and non-comic (mourning or indignation) for another.
